question: The owner: highlight 'the increasing frequency of major natural disasters and weather events due to climate change'. Which open data honestly show extremes becoming more frequent and more intense, the part attributed to climate change, and the toll of disasters on people, with what each can and cannot claim? Four angles (per degree of warming, observed series, disaster toll, attribution); adversarial verification; a critic on honesty and completeness.

research.scope: How much more often extremes happen per degree of warming (attributed, physical science): IPCC AR6 WGI Figure SPM.6 data on CEDA, Chapter 11 figure data, the IPCC Interactive Atlas, and World Bank CCKP extremes or warming-level products.
research.notes:
Bottom line: for 'how much more often per degree of warming, and how much is due to climate change', the strongest open dataset is the CEDA data for IPCC AR6 WGI Figure SPM.6 (doi:10.5285/93d1b84fbb144901809eaf67b35eb5c4, CC BY 4.0). It has 8 tiny CSVs, needs no login, and its values match the published figure exactly. Pair it with the SPM.3 data (doi:10.5285/dc6c126c95b1445d8e66d6b9f62054d4, CC BY 4.0) for the attributed observed-change headline (hot extremes up in 41 of 45 regions; human contribution high confidence in 23 and medium in 16). Neither has the reporting bias of disaster counts (EM-DAT) or the exposure bias of loss totals. Both are physical-climate measures, not counts of disasters or deaths, so the people toll (point 3) must still come from IDMC, Lancet and similar sources.

What each can claim. SPM.6 at 1 °C is the IPCC's model-based estimate of today's change compared with a climate without human influence. The published figure labels the 1 °C column 'Present' and says a once-a-decade heat extreme 'now likely occurs 2.8 times (1.8–3.2)'. Always say the values come from climate models and show the range. SPM.3 is a qualitative expert assessment. Count its categories; do not invent magnitudes.

For the home-page 1850-today timeline: no IPCC dataset gives an annual world series of extreme-event frequency from 1850. The honest options are (a) SPM.6 as a two-point annotation (1850-1900 = 1x, present ≈ 1.1 °C = 2.8x), not interpolated, with 1.5/2/4 °C shown separately as projections, not mapped to years; or (b) the CCKP ERA5 world series (1950-2025, CC BY 4.0, automatic API under the registered wb-cckp source). The CCKP 'GLOBAL' key seems to average over oceans as well (world tas 13.61 to 14.97 °C), and its rain indices are unreliable as trends. Use hot days or tropical nights, preferably per country.

Checked and not useful, or deferred:
- World Bank CCKP has no return-period or warming-level extremes products. The public S3 bucket s3://wbg-cckp/data/cmip6-x0.25/rx1day/ensemble-all-ssp245/ lists only anomaly, climatology, trend, timeseries, timeseriessmooth and yearofchange products by SSP and 20-year period.
- CEDA ch_11 holds only 6 Chapter 11 figures (11.3, 11.11, 11.11_A_1, 11.16, 11.19, FAQ 11.1), all NetCDF4 grids. The SPM.6 source figures (11.6, 11.7, 11.12, 11.15, 11.18) and the observed time series are not archived there.
- HadEX3 (Met Office) is under the Open Government Licence: 'HadEX3 is distributed under the Open Government Licence', from https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadex3/download_etccdi.html. It is gridded land extremes for 1901-2018 (v3.0.4). Its 'timeseries' zips (for example HadEX3_61-90_timeseries_TX90p.zip, 4.2 MB) contain only PNG plots, so a world series would need our own coverage-limited aggregation of NetCDF. It is a possible 1901-2018 observed 'warm days' line for another researcher to evaluate; I read no values.
- Wehner (2020) Mendeley data (doi:10.17632/xxpz35r97r.1) holds gridded land changes in 20-year return values at 1.5/2/3/4 °C. Its licence was not checked, and SPM.6 supersedes it.

Practical: SPM.6 can follow the ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm1 pattern exactly (same host, same licence wording, citation = CEDA 'Citable as' text plus the SPM citation). Watch for these file quirks:
- the panel folder layout differs from the Readme;
- the header reads '83th';
- trailing commas are inconsistent across files;
- the drought intensity file is a signed soil-moisture change (negative = drier);
- drought covers 17 drying regions only, not world land.

No files were written during this research; all fetches went to stdout or memory.

candidates.name: IPCC AR6 WGI Figure SPM.6 data: how much more often and how much stronger hot, wet and dry extremes get at 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 4 °C of warming
candidates.producer: IPCC Working Group I (data creators Chao Li, East China Normal University, and Mathias Hauser, ETH Zurich), supplied by the WGI Technical Support Unit and archived by the NERC EDS Centre for Environmental Data Analysis (CEDA). Citable as: Li, C.; Hauser, M. (2021), data for Figure SPM.6 (v20210809), doi:10.5285/93d1b84fbb144901809eaf67b35eb5c4, plus the IPCC 2021 SPM citation (doi:10.1017/9781009157896.001).
candidates.licence_quote: CEDA catalogue record (HTTP 200, 2026-10-12) and 00README_catalogue_and_licence.txt: "Use of these data is covered by the following licence(s): http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ When using these data you must cite them correctly using the citation given on the CEDA Data Catalogue record." License.txt: "This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License." metadata.yaml: "The data is made available under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)."
candidates.measures: CMIP6 multi-model change relative to 1850-1900 (1851-1900 for heat and rain) at global warming levels of 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0 and 4.0 °C. Each file gives the median plus the 17th/83rd (likely) and 5th/95th (very likely) percentiles. (a) Hottest day of the year over global land (TXx), 1-in-10-year event: frequency multiplier and intensity change in °C. (b) The same for the 1-in-50-year event. (c) Wettest day of the year over global land (Rx1day), 1-in-10-year event: frequency multiplier and intensity change in %. (d) Agricultural and ecological drought (annual total-column soil moisture below the 1850-1900 10th percentile) in 17 drying regions: frequency multiplier and intensity in standard deviations of soil moisture.
candidates.plain_phrase: A heat extreme that used to come once a decade in the 1850-1900 climate now comes about 2.8 times a decade at today's warming of about 1 °C. Climate models put it at about 4 times a decade at 1.5 °C, between 5 and 6 at 2 °C and about 9 at 4 °C. A once-in-50-years heat extreme now comes about 5 times as often, and would come about 39 times as often at 4 °C. Once-a-decade downpours already come about 1.3 times as often and carry about 7% more rain.
candidates.sample_values: I read all 8 CSVs from dap.ceda.ac.uk (each HTTP 200 with an ETag; Last-Modified 6 Aug 2021). Format: median (5th-95th). TXx 10-yr frequency: 1.0 °C 2.78 (1.81-3.22); 1.5 °C 4.11 (2.83-4.72); 2.0 °C 5.57 (3.77-6.03); 3.0 °C 8.12 (6.23-8.64); 4.0 °C 9.39 (8.25-9.63). TXx 10-yr intensity: +1.15, +1.88, +2.60, +3.91, +5.11 °C. TXx 50-yr frequency: 4.81 (2.28-6.37), 8.64, 13.92, 27.40, 39.19 (27.03-41.37). TXx 50-yr intensity: +1.20, +1.97, +2.70, +4.02, +5.28 °C. Rx1day 10-yr frequency: 1.32 (1.24-1.42), 1.53, 1.74, 2.21, 2.71 (2.31-3.58). Rx1day intensity: +6.68%, +10.52%, +14.04%, +21.30%, +30.22%. Drought 10-yr frequency: 1.70 (0.68-4.08), 2.04, 2.38, 3.23, 4.08 (1.70-7.21). Drought soil-moisture change: -0.32, -0.46, -0.57, -0.78, -0.99 SD (negative means drier). These match the published figure (IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM.pdf p.18), which labels the 1 °C column 'Present 1°C' with '2.8 times (1.8–3.2)'.
candidates.geography: World only. Heat and rain cover global land. Drought covers 17 AR6 'drying regions' (the Caribbean is excluded), so it is not a world-land figure. There are no country values.
candidates.years: Baseline 1850-1900 (1851-1900 for heat and rain). The dimension is global warming level, not calendar year. Dataset v20210809, published 2021-08-09; CEDA status 'Completed'; latest catalogue update 2024-03-09.
candidates.timeline_fit: This is not a time series and must not be stretched into one. On a 1850-today axis it can be an honest two-point annotation: 1850-1900 = once per decade (1x), and 'present' = 2.8x. IPCC itself labels the 1 °C column 'Present', and SPM A.1.2 gives 2011-2020 warming as 1.09 °C. The 1.5/2/3/4 °C values belong in a separate 'per degree of warming' panel and should not be mapped onto future years. Better as a home-page stat or step chart beside the timeline.
candidates.access: Automatic, no login: 8 tiny CSVs (189-211 bytes each) at https://dap.ceda.ac.uk/badc/ar6_wg1/data/spm/spm_06/v20210809/ under panel_a/TXx_freq_change_10_year_event.csv, panel_a/TXx_intens_change_10_year_event.csv, panel_b/TXx_freq_change_50_year_event.csv, panel_b/TXx_intens_change_50_year_event.csv, panel_c/Rx1day_freq_change_10_year_event.csv, panel_c/Rx1day_intens_change_10_year_event.csv, panel_d/drought_freq_change_10_year_event.csv and panel_d/drought_intens_change_10_year_event.csv. Also Readme_for_figure_SPM6.txt, metadata.yaml (full caption) and License.txt. The JSON listing is at https://data.ceda.ac.uk/badc/ar6_wg1/data/spm/spm_06/v20210809/?json. This is the same archive and access path as the registered ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm1.
candidates.already_registered: No. Sibling sources are registered: ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm1 (same CEDA archive, same CC BY 4.0 wording) and ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm (the SPM PDF, display-only).
candidates.already_researched: No. docs/research/sources-impacts.json covers the CEDA archive only through SPM.9 and SPM.1. Nothing in docs/ or pipeline/ mentions SPM.6.
candidates.caveats: Modelled (CMIP6 multi-model, mixed SSPs), not observed. Even the 1 °C value is a model estimate of today's human-caused change, not a count of real events. The published figure shows median and 5-95% (very likely) ranges; the files also carry 17-83% (likely) ranges. File quirks: the header says '83th'; trailing commas are inconsistent (the Rx1day intensity and drought files have none). The directory layout differs from the Readme: panel_b holds 50-year heat, panel_c rain and panel_d drought (the Readme puts rain in b and drought in c). The 3.0 °C row is in the data but not in the figure. The drought intensity file is the soil-moisture change (negative = drying), and its Readme lists the 83rd-percentile unit as '%' by mistake. The drought 95th percentile is non-monotonic (7.68 at 3 °C, 7.21 at 4 °C), and its 5th percentile at 1 °C is 0.68, so 'no increase' is inside the very likely range. Drought covers drying regions only. Frequency multipliers grow larger the rarer the event. Redraw from the CSVs; the IPCC figure image and design stay display-only under ipcc.ch/copyright. Cite both the CEDA dataset and the SPM.

candidates.name: IPCC AR6 WGI Figure SPM.3 data: observed change in hot extremes, heavy precipitation and agricultural/ecological drought since the 1950s, with confidence in human contribution, for 45 inhabited regions
candidates.producer: IPCC Working Group I (data creator Friederike Otto), archived by CEDA. Citable as: Otto, F.E.L.; Zhang, X.; Seneviratne, S.I. (2023), data for Figure SPM.3 (v20221116), doi:10.5285/dc6c126c95b1445d8e66d6b9f62054d4, plus the IPCC 2021 SPM citation.
candidates.licence_quote: CEDA catalogue record (HTTP 200, 2026-10-12) and 00README_catalogue_and_licence.txt: "Use of these data is covered by the following licence(s): http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ When using these data you must cite them correctly using the citation given on the CEDA Data Catalogue record."
candidates.measures: For each of 45 AR6 inhabited regions, two assessed categories. Type of observed change since the 1950s: Increase, Decrease, Low agreement in type of change, or Limited data and/or literature. Confidence in human contribution to that change: High, Medium, Low due to limited agreement, or Low due to limited evidence. Panels: (a) hot extremes, (b) heavy precipitation, (c) agricultural and ecological drought.
candidates.plain_phrase: Since the 1950s, hot extremes have increased in 41 of the world's 45 inhabited regions. Scientists have high or medium confidence that human-caused climate change contributed in 39 of them. Heavy rainfall has increased in 19 regions and drought in 12, but in many places the evidence for rain and drought is too thin to judge.
candidates.sample_values: I read SPM3_panel_a/b/c.csv (v20221116; ETag "6374ff57-ea3" for panel a) and counted the rows myself. Hot extremes: Increase 41/45 (human contribution High 23, Medium 16, Low due to limited agreement 2); Low agreement 2 (CNA, ENA); Limited data 2 (SSA, CAF). Heavy precipitation: Increase 19 (High 1 = NEU, Medium 1 = CNA, Low/limited agreement 17); Limited data 18; Low agreement 8. Drought: Increase 12 (Medium 2 = WNA, MED; Low 10); Decrease 1 (NAU); Low agreement 28; Limited data 4. The file comment reads 'years 1950 to 2021'.
candidates.geography: IPCC AR6 reference regions, not countries. Under the dashboard's world/country rule only the world-level counts (for example 41 of 45 regions) should be shown, not a regional map.
candidates.years: Observed change from the 1950s to the present (file comment: 1950 to 2021). Assessment published 2021. Data v20221116 is the latest of three versions (v20210809, v20220104, v20221116).
candidates.timeline_fit: None. This is a single assessment, so it suits a world stat card next to the timeline ('hot extremes up in 41 of 45 regions; human role high or medium confidence in 39').
candidates.access: Automatic, no login: https://dap.ceda.ac.uk/badc/ar6_wg1/data/spm/spm_03/v20221116/SPM3_panel_a.csv, SPM3_panel_b.csv and SPM3_panel_c.csv (BADC-CSV, 3.7-5.4 KB each).
candidates.already_registered: No (same CEDA archive as the registered ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm1).
candidates.already_researched: No.
candidates.caveats: Qualitative, expert-assessed categories, not magnitudes. 'Confidence in human contribution' is a confidence level, not the size of the contribution. Regions are unequal in size and population. For rain and drought, 'limited data' and 'low agreement' mean the evidence is missing, not that nothing changed. Present it as an IPCC assessment and do not compute any new statistic beyond simple counts. Redraw only; the IPCC hexagon figure is display-only.

candidates.name: World Bank CCKP ERA5 annual extremes indices (days at or above 35 °C and 40 °C, hottest day TXx, tropical nights at or above 26 °C, wettest day Rx1day, days with 20 mm or more of rain), world and every country, 1950-2025
candidates.producer: World Bank Group, Climate Change Knowledge Portal, from Copernicus C3S ERA5 reanalysis
candidates.licence_quote: "Unless specifically labeled otherwise, these Datasets are provided to you under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0), with the additional terms below." I reused this from the registered pipeline/sources/wb-cckp.yaml (checked 2026-10-04) and did not re-fetch it: climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch today.
candidates.measures: Annual ERA5 0.25° values aggregated by CCKP to 'GLOBAL' and to 246 countries. hd35/hd40: days with daily maximum at or above 35/40 °C. txx: hottest daily maximum of the year (°C). tr26: nights with minimum above 26 °C. rx1day: largest one-day rainfall (mm). r20mm: days with 20 mm or more.
candidates.plain_phrase: In the reanalysis, the average place on Earth now gets about 11 days a year above 35 °C, against about 8 in 1950-1979. Very warm nights have roughly doubled.
candidates.sample_values: I read these from the API on 2026-10-12. GLOBAL hd35: 6.88 (1950), mean 7.85 (1950-79), mean 11.10 (2016-25), 12.23 (2024), 11.17 (2025). hd40: mean 1.68, then 2.98, with 3.42 in 2024. txx: mean 20.52 °C, then 21.58 °C. tr26: mean 24.12 nights, then 52.11, with 66.99 in 2024. rx1day: mean 17.08 mm, then 20.04 mm. r20mm: mean 7.82 days, then 9.46. Country hd35, 1950 and 2025: Nigeria 76.66 and 143.67; USA 6.21 and 12.49; Pakistan 98.98 and 123.68; India 61.55 and 67.95.
candidates.geography: World and 246 countries/territories (all_countries endpoint).
candidates.years: 1950-2025 annual (keys 'YYYY-07'); one year is added each year.
candidates.timeline_fit: Yes, for 1950 to today: a 76-point world annual line, starting 100 years after the axis begins. It shows observed change, not attribution. Hot-day and tropical-night counts are the most robust; avoid the rain indices on a headline timeline.
candidates.access: Automatic JSON API with no key. URL pattern: https://cckpapi.worldbank.org/cckp/v1/era5-x0.25_timeseries_{hd35|hd40|txx|tr26|rx1day|rx5day|r20mm|hd30}_timeseries_annual_1950-2025_mean_historical_era5_x0.25_mean/{global|all_countries}?_format=json. The registered wb-cckp client and User-Agent already work.
candidates.already_registered: The source wb-cckp is registered, but only for ERA5 tas and CMIP6 hd35 projections. These ERA5 extremes artifacts are not registered.
candidates.already_researched: Partly. CCKP is in sources-country-and-local.json for temperature; I found no research on the ERA5 extremes series.
candidates.caveats: The 'GLOBAL' aggregate appears to average over the whole globe, oceans included: the same endpoint gives ERA5 tas of 13.61 °C (1950) and 14.97 °C (2025), a land-plus-ocean mean. A world 'hot days' value is therefore diluted by ocean cells. Confirm CCKP's definition before labelling, or use country values. ERA5 rainfall trends are affected by changes in the observations fed into the reanalysis over time, so Rx1day and r20mm trends are not reliable as headline evidence. Reanalysis is not station data. The series shows the trend, not how much is due to climate change. The URL period code changes each year. There are no warming-level or return-period products: an S3 listing of wbg-cckp CMIP6 rx1day/rx5day shows only climatology, anomaly, trend, timeseries and yearofchange products by SSP and 20-year period.

research.scope: Observed long time series of how often extreme weather happens, for the whole world, ideally running from the early 1900s or 1950s to recent years, for a home-page timeline row. Datasets checked: HadEX3, GHCNDEX (both via Climdex), ERA5-based C3S products, IGCC 2025 extremes indicators, Lancet Countdown 1.2.2 drought and 1.2.3 extreme precipitation, and the NOAA US Climate Extremes Index.
research.notes:
WHICH SERIES HONESTLY SHOW AN INCREASE, AND FROM WHEN (all observed trends; none of them is attribution by itself):
1. IGCC marine heatwave days, ERA5 1940-2025: flat at about 12-18 days a year until the late 1970s, rising from the early 1980s, record in 2024 (ERA5 87.9 days; four-product mean 81.4). The IGCC paper says the count more than tripled between 1991 and 2025. Best world timeline candidate. Open (CC BY 4.0), on an already-registered source (igcc-2025), just needs a new artifact.
2. IGCC land TXx (hottest day of the year), ERA5 1950-2025: strong rise from about 1980; the 2016-2025 decade is 1.92 °C above 1850-1900. Open. It shows intensity, not frequency.
3. Lancet 1.2.2 extreme drought, share of land 1951-2024: about 10-20% until the mid-1990s, then rising to a record 60.7% in 2024. Noncommercial; source already registered, new artifact. The 1950s were also dry, so the 'increase' is a post-late-1990s story.
4. Lancet 1.2.3 extreme precipitation, 1961-1990 and 1995-2024: from 3.67 to 4.33 events a year (decade means), record 4.97 in 2024. Noncommercial. Reanalysis precipitation, and there are no values for 1991-94.
5. NOAA CEI, US only, 1910-2025: rises from the 2010s (about 31-33% against about 15-20%). Public domain.
6. HadEX3 (ends 2018) and GHCNDEX (1951-2026): open (OGL; CC BY 4.0), but neither publishes a world-average file. A world line would be our own area-weighted calculation, labelled as such, with the caveat that coverage changes over time. GHCNDEX is the only station-based extremes product current to 2026.

CHECKED AND NOT SUITABLE AS A TIMELINE:
- Copernicus C3S Global Climate Highlights 2025 Fig. 11: a single-year ERA5-HEAT map. '50% of the globe (land areas; excluding Antarctica) experienced more days than average with at least strong heat stress' in 2025 against 1991-2020. No long world series.
- C3S Climate Indicators page: no extremes indicators.
- C3S Interactive Atlas dataset (CDS multi-origin-c3s-atlas, licence CC-BY-4.0 per the CDS API): ERA5 TX35, TX40, Rx1day and SPEI6 as monthly grids, 1940-2025. A world series would need computing or a manual viewer export. No values read.
- Climdex's own global plots are PNG only. The 'images/...timeseries...zip' files on the HadEX3 download page are PNGs, not data.
- BAMS State of the Climate extremes figures: no open figure-data file found; AMS terms not checked.

ATTRIBUTION (the owner's 'due to climate change'): pair these trend rows with registered attribution sources, never with a claim that the trend itself is attributed. Options: IPCC AR6 SPM (registered ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm; SPM.6 frequency multipliers by warming level are labelled projections); IGCC human-induced warming (registered); Lancet 1.1.1 attributable heatwave days (registered); Carbon Brief (no-derivatives). The marine heatwave attribution figure (Frölicher et al. 2018, '87 per cent of MHWs are attributable') exists only in Carbon Brief's no-derivatives table and a closed Nature paper.

PRACTICAL: for the marine heatwave series, use the ERA5 column as the one series and the four-product mean (1982-) as a twin, never the 'mean' column across 1981/82. research.scope: MAJOR DISASTERS AND THEIR TOLL ON PEOPLE (counts, deaths, people affected or displaced; world and country), with what each source can and cannot claim
research.notes:
What the data can honestly support for the owner's ask:
(1) 'More frequent' cannot be shown from disaster-impact counts. EM-DAT-based counts (CRED reports, the WMO Atlas) rise largely because reporting improved; WMO and CRED say so in print. IDMC's event rows went from 164 (2008) to 7,042 (2025) and drought starts only in 2017. NOAA's billion-dollar count rises partly with exposure and wealth. Frequency and intensity claims should come from physical-hazard datasets (other angles: IPCC SPM.1 data, Lancet heatwave days, drought share, wildfire).
(2) 'Due to climate change' for the human toll: Newman & Noy 2023 (CC BY; use only the printed statements, because the CC0 deposit embeds an EM-DAT sheet), the registered Lancet 1.1.5 heat-death indicator, and the registered Carbon Brief map. The Imperial/LSHTM summer-2025 European heat-death report (16,500 of 24,400 deaths attributable across 854 cities) is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 per its Imperial SPIRAL record (doi:10.25560/123873; dc.rights 'Creative Commons Attribution-Non-Commercial-No-Derivatives 4.0'), not CC BY as search summaries claim. It is city-based (about 30% of Europe's population), so it does not fit the world/country rule anyway.
(3) Toll on people: there is NO open world toll series reaching back toward 1850. The longest open series are IDMC (world, 2008-2025, noncommercial), NWS weather fatalities (US, 1940-2025, public domain) and NOAA billion-dollar disasters (US, 1980-2024, public domain). The new find is CRED's own annual 'Disasters in Numbers' reports. The 2024 and 2025 editions are CC BY 4.0, and the 2021-2023 editions say free or unrestricted use with citation. They allow EM-DAT's published world totals (deaths, affected, losses, counts by hazard, latest year vs 20-year average) to be shown and transcribed with page locators, while the EM-DAT database stays rejected. CRED's disclaimer keeps the underlying data under EM-DAT terms. Keep each edition as its own vintage.
Corrections and flags for the registry: (a) idmc-gidd.yaml says the GIDD page has no button for the disaster event export. IDMC's website bundle (release-website-components.idmcdb.org/js/main.bundle.js) builds that link (gidd/disasters/disaster-export/ with hazard_type__in) when Cause = disaster, and also offers 'Disaster events aggregated data (.xlsx)'. A person should confirm this in a browser; it would allow manual acquisition of the hazard split now. (b) IDMC licence re-read 2026-10-12: unchanged (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO). (c) IDMC event-file hazard sums do not equal GRID 2026's printed hazard totals (drought 322,809 vs 529,000), so never mix the two. (d) The NOAA archive and the per-year CSV (time-series/US/1980-2024.csv) still answer 200, but the page is unmaintained: mirror it now.
Death tolls for the same year differ by compiler (2025: CRED 16,607 without heat deaths; Munich Re about 17,200; Aon about 42,000 including more than 25,000 heat deaths per press coverage). The site must never mix compilers in one series.
Not usable or not assessed: Swiss Re sigma (403 to scripts; proprietary), Aon and Gallagher Re (proprietary; values seen only in press coverage), Munich Re (conflicting terms; needs permission). WMO Atlas and WMO State of the Global Climate are display-only (short extracts). UNDRR GAR, DesInventar and the Sendai Monitor sit behind a Cloudflare 403 and have no clear data licence. Global Flood Database (Tellman 2021: exposure, not toll, 2000-2018) is labelled CC BY-NC 4.0 only in the Earth Engine catalog; its producer site is client-rendered and the paper is paywalled. The Dartmouth Flood Observatory archive (deaths and displaced per flood, 1985-) timed out on 2026-10-12. The GDACS terms URL returned 404. Climate Central's continuation of billion-dollar disasters is already researched (noncommercial; bulk download prohibited). EM-DAT's FAIR archive (CC BY-NC-ND) cannot supply yearly sums even under the no-derivatives class, because summing is a recalculation.

research.scope: Attribution of extreme events to climate change: how much more likely or intense specific events, or classes of events, were because of human-caused warming. Covers World Weather Attribution, ClimaMeter, Carbon Brief, BAMS Explaining Extreme Events, State of Wildfires 2025-26, impact-attribution datasets (Clarke/Otto, Newman & Noy), Met Office and Copernicus products, the Lancet attributable heatwave days, plus two IPCC AR6 CEDA datasets and one CC BY Nature paper not yet in the registry.
research.notes:
BOTTOM LINE ON HONESTY. No attribution source provides a world time series on a 1850-today axis. Attribution answers 'how much more likely or intense', for an event or a class of events, against a 1850-1900 baseline. The closest things to a trend 'due to climate change' are: (a) Quilcaille et al. 2025, CC BY 4.0, with decade medians for recorded deadly heatwaves: about 20x more likely in 2000-2009 and about 200x in 2010-2019; intensity +1.4 C, then +1.7 C, then +2.2 C (2020-2023). (b) Lancet 1.1.1 (registered), attributable heatwave days per person, 2020-2024 only (14.2 to 25.8). (c) IPCC SPM.6 (CC BY via CEDA, not yet registered), which turns the existing temperature line into odds of extremes per degree of warming: a 10-year hot extreme happens 2.78x as often at 1 C, 4.11x at 1.5 C and 9.39x at 4 C. Suggested home-page treatment: keep the temperature line as the timeline. Put a 'what each degree does to extremes' panel (SPM.6) beside it, and recent-decade markers (Quilcaille decade bars, Lancet 2020-2024) at the right-hand end. Never map warming levels onto years, and never splice series together. Use SPM.3 as the 'observed and attributed' summary card: hot extremes up in 41 of 45 regions (39 with medium or high confidence of human cause), against only 19 for heavy rain and 12 for drought (mostly low confidence). That keeps the weaker signals visible.

LICENCE FINDINGS. WWA's Spiral deposits are CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (48 of 106 items found; a few are CC BY-NC; journal papers are CC BY), and the WWA site itself states no licence and offers no results table. ClimaMeter is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 on its disclaimer page. BAMS EEE is AMS copyright, not CC, and ametsoc.org refuses scripts. Carbon Brief offers no other licence on the page or the CSV. Its own printed counts by type (Heat 261, Rain & flooding 223, Drought 121, Storm 84 and so on) and by finding (743/76/81/67) can be quoted verbatim. It publishes no counts by year (only 'around 50' in the first decade and 'more than 500' in the next), and counting CSV rows by year would be an ND adaptation that measures research effort anyway. Met Office website content is OGL v3: the UK 2025 record was about 260x more likely, about a 3-year event now against about 780 years pre-industrial. Quote it from the news text because of the OGL 'underlying documents' exclusion. Copernicus C3S has no attribution data product yet: tender C3S2_451 for an operational attribution service and office was published 9 Jul 2024, and the 2026 tenders C3S2_452 and C3S2_610 are still building it. Clarke/Otto impact attribution: no open structured dataset found. The Imperial/LSHTM rapid heat-death reports (for example 'Summer heat deaths in 854 European cities more than tripled due to climate change', 17 Sep 2025) are CC BY-NC-ND on Spiral and not peer-reviewed. Their 16,469 of 24,404 deaths figure came from search results and was not read in the PDF. The Exevada attribution database (github.com/C3S-attribution-service/exevada) is Apache-2.0 software with no data, last pushed 2021. Climate Central CSI is already researched as noncommercial (allowed class, manual download only).

OWNER DECISIONS NEEDED. (1) EM-DAT-derived values inside open-labelled papers or deposits. Quilcaille's SI carries EM-DAT event IDs; the Newman, Panwar & Noy Dataverse workbook (CC0 label) contains a full 7,404-row EM-DAT sheet. Recommendation: for Quilcaille, publish only the authors' own attribution numbers (decade medians, or country, year, intensity and probability ratio), with no EM-DAT fields and no event download. Reject the Newman deposit under the jones-2025 'downstream label cannot lift upstream terms' rule unless CRED agrees. (2) Leave out every carbon-major column in Quilcaille (Carbon Majors is already rejected). (3) Quilcaille's text says the largest intensity change (+2.9 C) was the 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave, but the SI gives USA 2021-0390 at +2.73 C and the +2.91 C maximum is Slovakia 2023-0438. verdicts.values_checked: Every candidate value matches the CSVs, given as median (5th-95th). TXx 10-yr frequency: 2.78 (1.81-3.22), 4.11, 5.57, 8.12, 9.39 (8.25-9.63). TXx 10-yr intensity: 1.15, 1.88, 2.60, 3.91, 5.11 C. TXx 50-yr frequency: 4.81 (2.28-6.37), 8.64, 13.92, 27.40, 39.19 (27.03-41.37). TXx 50-yr intensity: 1.20 to 5.28 C. Rx1day frequency: 1.32 (1.24-1.42) to 2.71 (2.31-3.58). Rx1day intensity: 6.68 to 30.22 %. Drought frequency: 1.70 (0.68-4.08) to 4.08 (1.70-7.21). Soil-moisture change: -0.32 to -0.99 SD. I streamed the SPM PDF (IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM.pdf, HTTP 200, 3,361,797 bytes) in memory. On p.18 it prints 'Present 1°C', 'Once now likely occurs 2.8 times (1.8–3.2)', '+1.2°C hotter', '+6.7% wetter' and 'occurs 1.7 times (0.7–4.1)' for drought. Its caption calls 1850-1900 'a climate without human influence'. Corrections: (1) The catalogue abstract and metadata.yaml map panels a-d exactly to the directories. Only the Readme is out of date (it puts rain in b and drought in c). (2) Drought is computed over 16 regions: 17 drying regions are listed, but the caption says the Caribbean 'is not included in the calculation'. (3) At 1 C the soil-moisture 83rd percentile is +0.01 and the 95th is +0.19, so even the likely range includes no drying. The 5th percentile also runs non-monotonic (-2.23 at 3 C, -2.03 at 4 C). (4) SPM A.1.2 puts 2011-2020 at 1.09 C, so 'present' in 2021 meant about 2011-2020. The repo's own IGCC 2025 indicator (data/v1/indicators/warming.igcc-2025.human-induced-2025.json) puts human-induced warming in 2025 at 1.37 C. So '1 C = today' is wrong for a site published in 2026.
verdicts.honest_wording: MAY say: 'Climate models assessed by the IPCC (AR6, 2021) estimate that a heat extreme that came once a decade in 1850-1900 comes about 2.8 times a decade (very likely 1.8-3.2) at 1 C of global warming, the level the IPCC called present (about 2011-2020). The IPCC treats 1850-1900 as a climate without human influence. The same extreme would come 4.1 times a decade at 1.5 C, 5.6 at 2 C and 9.4 at 4 C. A once-in-50-years heat extreme comes 4.8 times as often at 1 C and 39 times as often at 4 C. Over land, the once-a-decade wettest day comes 1.3 times as often and is about 7% wetter at 1 C, and 2.7 times as often and about 30% wetter at 4 C. In regions projected to dry, a once-a-decade soil-moisture drought comes 1.7 times as often at 1 C (range 0.7-4.1, so no increase cannot be ruled out) and 4.1 times as often at 4 C.' Label it as modelled and cite both the CEDA dataset and the SPM. Show the 'per degree of warming' values in their own panel or step chart. MAY NOT: present these as counts of observed events; call the 1 C column 'today' (the world is at about 1.37 C of human-caused warming, IGCC 2025, between the 1 and 1.5 C columns, and no value for 1.37 C may be interpolated); map warming levels onto calendar years; draw it as a 1850-today time series; call the drought numbers global (they cover 16 drying regions); reuse the IPCC figure artwork. The 3.0 C row is real data but is not in the published figure, so say so if it is shown.
verdicts.evidence: I read the CEDA catalogue page (licence, citation, status, the abstract's panel-to-file mapping, and the note that 'a negative soil moisture change corresponds to a positive drying signal'). I read License.txt, the Readme (author Mathias Hauser; it lists the 83rd-percentile drought intensity unit as '%', a typo) and metadata.yaml (full caption, including the 16-region note). I read all 8 CSVs with their headers. From the SPM PDF I read p.18 (the SPM.6 labels and caption) and p.15 (B.2.2: 'every additional 0.5°C of global warming causes clearly discernible increases in the intensity and frequency of hot extremes ... (very likely), and heavy precipitation (high confidence)'). Nothing in docs/sources.md, pipeline/sources or docs/research mentions WGI SPM.6; the SPM.6 hits in sources-solutions-and-action.json are WGIII. Claim strength: projection by warming level, with attribution framing from the IPCC baseline. A strong source.

verdicts.honest_wording: MAY say: 'The IPCC (AR6, 2021) assessed that since the 1950s hot extremes have increased in 41 of the world's 45 inhabited regions. In 23 it has high confidence, and in 16 medium confidence, that human influence contributed. Heavy rainfall has increased in 19 regions, but at regional scale confidence in a human contribution is mostly low; in 18 regions there are too few data to judge. Agricultural and ecological drought has increased in 12 regions and decreased in 1; the evidence is mixed in 28 and too thin in 4.' It may sit beside SPM A.3.1, quoted verbatim: 'virtually certain that hot extremes (including heatwaves) have become more frequent and more intense across most land regions since the 1950s ... with high confidence that human-induced climate change is the main driver'. MAY NOT: present the categories as magnitudes or as a time series; say regions without 'Increase' saw no change ('limited data' and 'low agreement' mean the evidence is missing or mixed); treat confidence levels as the size of the human contribution; map the regions as countries or compute regional or area-weighted statistics (under the world/country rule only world-level counts may be shown); present the 39 as a number the IPCC printed (say 'counted from the IPCC data'); reuse the hexagon artwork.
verdicts.evidence: I read the CEDA catalogue page (licence, citation, abstract 'synthesis of assessed observed and attributable regional changes', version and status), License.txt and the Readme. I parsed all three v20221116 CSVs. From the SPM PDF I read the p.10-11 figure tallies and caption ('All assessments are made for each region as a whole and for the 1950s to the present') and p.8 A.3.1/A.3.2. This is the attribution evidence the owner's ask needs most, and it is open (CC BY 4.0) in the same archive as the registered ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm1. It is a single assessment with no timeline, so it fits a stat card.

verdicts.name: World Bank CCKP ERA5 annual extremes indices (days above 35 C and 40 C, hottest day TXx, tropical nights above 26 C, wettest day Rx1day, days with more than 20 mm of rain), world and every country, 1950-2025
verdicts.licence_quote: World Bank Data Catalog record for this collection (dataset 0065626, the landing page of DOI 10.57966/128g-6s70, 'Climate Change Knowledge Portal: Observed Climate Data, ERA5 0.25-degree'; HTTP 200, 2026-10-12): 'License : Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 This dataset is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0'. World Bank Dataset Terms (re-fetched today, HTTP 200): 'Unless specifically labeled otherwise, these Datasets are provided to you under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0), with the additional terms below.'
verdicts.data_access_checked: The API needs no key. With the pipeline's User-Agent, https://cckpapi.worldbank.org/cckp/v1/era5-x0.25_timeseries_{var}_timeseries_annual_1950-2025_mean_historical_era5_x0.25_mean/{global|global_land|all_countries}?_format=json returned HTTP/2 200 application/json, with no ETag or Last-Modified. Each response has 76 annual values keyed YYYY-07; all_countries has 246 entries. climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org returns 403 to curl, even with a browser User-Agent. The licence was therefore confirmed on the World Bank's own Data Catalog page for the ERA5 0.25 collection, whose description says data are 'available as API or xls via https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/download-data', and on the Dataset Terms. The Dataset Terms carry the 'Exceptions for Some Third-Party Data' clause and a duty to pass the attribution requirement on to anyone the data are shared with; neither forbids derivatives, and the registered wb-cckp entry already handles both. CCKP's GitHub docs define hd35 as 'Number of Hot Days (Tmax > 35°C)', hd40 as 'Tmax > 40°C', tr26 as 'T-min > 26°C' and r20mm as 'Precipitation >20mm'. All are strictly greater-than, not 'at or above'.
verdicts.values_checked: The GLOBAL values match the candidate. hd35: 6.88 (1950), 7.85 (1950-79 mean), 11.10 (2016-25 mean), 12.23 (2024), 11.17 (2025). hd40: 1.68 to 2.98. txx: 20.52 to 21.58 C. tr26: 24.12 to 52.11, with 66.99 in 2024. rx1day: 17.08 to 20.04 mm. r20mm: 7.82 to 9.46. Countries, hd35 in 1950 and 2025: NGA 76.66 and 143.67; USA 6.21 and 12.49; PAK 98.98 and 123.68; IND 61.55 and 67.95. CORRECTION: GLOBAL includes the oceans. Its tas is 13.61 C (1950), while a GLOBAL_LAND aggregate at /global_land gives 9.36 C. A land-only world series therefore exists, and it gives very different numbers (1950-79 mean, then 2016-25 mean): hd35 30.33 to 41.73 days (2024: 45.31); hd40 6.60 to 11.10; tr26 9.83 to 19.66; txx 25.14 to 26.86 C; rx1day 15.41 to 16.40 mm (+6.4%); r20mm 6.38 to 7.16. The candidate's world sentence ('about 11 days a year above 35 C against about 8') is the ocean-diluted figure. The candidate's 'doubling' of warm nights in GLOBAL is probably dominated by tropical ocean air crossing the 26 C threshold; this is plausible but I have not confirmed it. Its single-year country comparisons (1950 against 2025) are cherry-pick-prone.
verdicts.honest_wording: MAY say, using GLOBAL_LAND and multi-year means: 'In the ERA5 reanalysis, as aggregated by the World Bank, the average spot on land had about 42 days a year above 35 C in 2016-2025, against about 30 in 1950-1979. Days above 40 C rose from about 7 to 11, and nights that stay above 26 C roughly doubled, from about 10 to 20.' Country lines are fine with 10-year or 30-year averages. Label it as 'reanalysis (model and observations combined), observed trend'. Attribution must come from SPM.3 or SPM.6, not from this series. MAY NOT: use the GLOBAL (ocean-included) aggregate as 'the average place on Earth'; say the series shows how much is due to climate change; headline rx1day or r20mm (ERA5 rainfall is model-generated, and its trends shift as the observing system changes); describe it as weather-station records; extend it before 1950 on the 1850 axis; compare single years; write 'at or above 35 C' (the definition is strictly above).
verdicts.evidence: I fetched the API for GLOBAL, GLOBAL_LAND and all_countries for tas, hd35, hd40, tr26, txx, rx1day and r20mm and computed the means myself. GLOBAL_LAND was found by probing: WLD, world and all_regions return empty data. I read the World Bank Data Catalog page (licence, and a description still saying 1950-2022, now stale), the Dataset Terms page, the AWS Open Data registry entry (lists CC BY 4.0) and the CCKP GitHub docs (variable definitions). The wb-cckp source is registered; these indices are not. ERA5 before 1979 relies on fewer observations, so early values in data-sparse countries (e.g. Nigeria) are less certain. That is a general reanalysis caveat, not checked against an ECMWF statement today. Use it only as observed-trend context, with GLOBAL_LAND replacing GLOBAL.

I streamed the Zenodo zip (1,495,354 bytes) into memory. Its member ClimateIndicator-data-0f2765d/data/base/marine_heatwave_days/MHW_days_per_year_combined.csv has the same sha256 as the raw GitHub file (77c166c891c79782...). The zip also holds the CDS-format files: '...marine_input-datasets_datasets-all_annual-mean-timeseries_IGCC-2025a.csv' (4,952 bytes, long format by dataset) and '...marine_igcc-assessment_synthesis_annual-mean-timeseries_IGCC-2025a.csv' (958 bytes). The synthesis file is the 'mean' column, i.e. the producer's own spliced series. The README credits the indicator to Catherine Gregory and Thomas Frölicher.
verdicts.values_checked: Read 2026-10-12. Columns: time,timebound_lower,timebound_upper,OISST,OSTIA,CRW,ERA5,mean. ERA5: 1940 21.16; 1959 10.68; 1960 13.22; 1980 24.91; 1981 22.83; 1982 30.47; 2000 28.93; 2016 65.9; 2023 77.68; 2024 87.88; 2025 75.5. Mean column: 1981 22.83 (ERA5 alone), 1982 22.29 (four products), 2000 19.66, 2016 58.34, 2023 71.44, 2024 81.42, 2025 64.9. My calculations: ERA5 averaged 31.7 over 1985-2014, against 25.5 for the four-product mean over the same years, so ERA5 runs about 6 days higher. The splice in the synthesis series therefore makes the early (ERA5-only) years look high compared with the later years and understates the rise. Four-product mean for 2016-2025 is 58.2, which matches the paper's '58 d'. ERA5 for 2016-2025 is 65.4. Paper text checked: 99th percentile, 11-day window, 1985-2014 climatology, offset to 1850-1900 using ERSST v6, only 60S-60N, 2023/2024/2025 four-product means of 70/82/65 days, 2016-2025 (58 d) against 2007-2016 (36 d), and 'more than tripled between 1991 and 2025'.
verdicts.honest_wording: MAY say: 'Marine heatwave days: on average across the ocean between 60°S and 60°N, the number of days a year when sea surface temperature was above a local extreme threshold (the daily 99th percentile, set from 1985-2014 and shifted to the 1850-1900 level). In the ERA5 reanalysis the average was about 12-18 days a year in every decade from the 1940s to the 1970s. It was 65 days a year in 2016-2025, and 2024 set the record at 88 days. Averaged over four datasets, 2016-2025 had 58 days a year against 36 in 2007-2016, and 2024 had 82 (IGCC 2025).' Chart the ERA5 column as one line for 1940-2025. The four-product mean may be shown as a separate line from 1982. Label the series 'observed trend'. For the 'due to climate change' part, pair it with the separately sourced IPCC AR6 WGI SPM statement A.3.1 (registered ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm). A.3.1 says marine heatwaves roughly doubled in frequency since the 1980s (high confidence) and human influence very likely contributed to most of them since at least 2006. Credit the attribution to IPCC, not to this file. MAY NOT: say 'each patch of ocean' spends two months in a heatwave, since it is a spatial average and some regions get far more and others far less. Do not chart the 'mean' or synthesis column as one continuous 1940-2025 line, because it switches from ERA5 to a four-product mean in 1982. Do not mix ERA5 early values with four-product recent values in one comparison. Do not present the series itself as attribution. Do not describe it as weather on land, or as country data.
verdicts.evidence: The licence is the producer's own and has three independent confirmations: the ESSD Sect. 13 sentence, the Zenodo record licence (cc-by-4.0) and the GitHub repo licence (CC-BY-4.0). The data file is byte-identical between raw GitHub at the pinned commit and the DOI-pinned Zenodo zip. No clause forbids redistribution or derivatives. Inputs: ERA5 (Copernicus licence, attribution required, e.g. 'contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information'), OISST and CRW (NOAA, public domain), OSTIA (Copernicus Marine/Met Office, attribution). The trend is real and consistent across products: all four datasets rise from the early 1980s. Claim strength is observed-trend-not-attributed: the paper says only that it is consistent with ocean surface warming. Attribution comes from AR6 SPM A.3.1, which I verified from the IPCC SPM PDF. Caveats: pre-satellite ERA5 SST is less certain; El Niño years spike; values depend on the threshold and offset method (Supplement Fig. S15). New artifact on the existing igcc-2025 entry; the yaml comment 'we do not use the extremes files' would need updating.

verdicts.name: Lancet Countdown 2025 indicator 1.2.2: share of world land area in extreme drought

Months keys: 1m, 3m, 6m, 12m. 1m: 1951 19.24; 1952 19.32; 1956 10.77; 1971 9.05; 1983 22.45; 1998 40.11; 2010 45.22; 2015 46.00; 2020 50.33; 2022 42.79; 2023 52.32; 2024 60.69. verdicts.honest_wording: MAY say: 'Share of the world's land with at least one month of extreme meteorological drought in the year (SPEI-6, against 1986-2005). It was about 15% a year in the 1950s, rose from the late 1990s, and reached a record 60.7% in 2024 (Lancet Countdown 2025, indicator 1.2.2).' Label it as an estimated index from gridded station data. MAY add that SPEI counts evaporative demand, so warmer air itself pushes the index towards drought. For attribution, use only the separately sourced IPCC AR6 SPM A.3.2: human-induced change has contributed to increases in agricultural and ecological droughts in some regions (medium confidence). MAY NOT: call it 'drought caused by climate change', or say it means crop or water shortages or people affected. Do not chart the 12-month threshold (NA gaps). Do not splice it with the 2026-report vintage due 28 Oct 2026. Do not use it on a commercial page (NC licence; share-alike applies to derived data files).
verdicts.evidence: The producer's own licence is in the data file itself (DATA GUIDANCE 2.2) and on use-our-data, which I re-read today. CC BY-NC-SA allows derivatives and charts on this non-commercial site, with share-alike for derived data. Upstream SPEIbase is ODbL per the earlier verified research (sources-impacts.json verdict 15), so credit CSIC/SPEI as well. Values reproduce the producer's key finding exactly. The trend is observed but not attributed: the producer uses it to show change, not cause. Early decades and Africa have thinner CRU station coverage. It is a new artifact on the registered lancet-countdown-2025 entry.

# Critic report: showing more frequent and more intense extremes, and the share due to climate change

I spot-checked the key numbers against the producers' own files:
- the IGCC repo at commit `0f2765dc…`;
- the ESSD paper, doi:10.5194/essd-18-3889-2026, Section 10.2;
- the CEDA data for Figures SPM.3 (version v20221116) and SPM.6 (version v20210809).

Registry context:
- `/Users/apple/Documents/GitHub/environment dashboard/pipeline/sources/ipcc-ar6-wg1-spm.yaml` is **display-only**. So statement A.3.1 can only be quoted word for word, never turned into data. The counts and values have to come from the CC BY 4.0 data on CEDA.
- `/Users/apple/Documents/GitHub/environment dashboard/pipeline/sources/igcc-2025.yaml` currently says "we do not use the extremes files". That entry needs amending before the marine heatwave or TXx files are used.

## 1(a) Home-page timeline row

**Recommended row: marine heatwave days per year, world ocean between 60°S and 60°N.**
- Source: IGCC 2025. File `data/base/marine_heatwave_days/MHW_days_per_year_combined.csv`, **ERA5 column only**, 1940-2025. It sits inside the registered `igcc-2025` deposit, which is open (CC BY 4.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21494229).
- Why this one: it is the only world series published by its producer that directly measures **how often** extremes happen and runs most of the axis. The producer says ERA5 "exhibits similar variability during the pre-satellite era".
- Values I checked (ERA5 decade means): 1940s 15.5, 1950s 12.1, 1960s 15.4, 1970s 17.9, 1980s 27.4, 2000s 33.1, 2010s 49.4. 2016-2025 averages 65.4.
- **Traced number: 2024 = 87.88 days in the ERA5 column, the record.** Footnote the producer's headline separately: "maximum mean of 82 MHW days in 2024", which is the mean of four datasets. Never mix 82 into the ERA5 line.
- **Leave 1850-1939 empty**, labelled "no daily global sea-surface data". The method subtracts an 1850-1900 offset (via ERSST v6), but no pre-industrial value is printed. Do not draw a "3.65 days" baseline yourself.
- **Caveats to show:**
  - 1940-41 run high (21.2 and 20.5 days), probably affected by the known wartime sea-temperature measurement bias. Do not read those years as real heatwaves.
  - ERA5 sits above the satellite products where they overlap (2024: OISST 78.8 against ERA5 87.9), so always write "in ERA5".
  - The `mean` column, and the synthesis file, switch to a four-dataset mean in 1982. They must never be charted as one continuous line.
- **The "due to climate change" part is an annotation, not data in the row.** Quote A.3.1 as display-only text: "approximately doubled in frequency since the 1980s (high confidence) … human influence has very likely contributed to most of them since at least 2006." Credit it to the IPCC.

**Land alternative, if the owner insists on land:** IGCC TXx (the hottest day of each year), ERA5 column, 1950-2025.
- Decadal means relative to 1850-1900: 2000-2009 is 1.21 °C, 2016-2025 is 1.92 °C.
- This measures **how hot**, not **how often**. Use only the ERA5 column: Berkeley Earth's input is CC BY-NC and its products are already parked in the registry, and HadEX3 (the third column) is under the Open Government Licence.

**What not to put on the home row:**
- **World Bank CCKP "global land" days above 35 °C.** It is an average over land area, so hot deserts dominate it, not the places people live. Use it on country pages with 10-year means.
- **Lancet 1.2.2 drought (60.7% of land in 2024).** It sits uneasily with the IPCC assessment in SPM.3 panel c, explained below. The figure counts land with at least one month of extreme SPEI-6 drought, and that metric depends heavily on how evaporation is modelled. Drill-down only, and always shown with the IPCC context.

## 1(b) Drill-down views

1. **"What each degree of warming does"** (open, IPCC AR6 Figure SPM.6 data on CEDA, CC BY 4.0, labelled "modelled, CMIP6"):
   - For a once-a-decade hot extreme of 1850-1900, the median at 1 °C is 2.78 times as often. The likely range (17th-83rd percentile) is 2.24-3.05; the very likely range (5th-95th) is 1.81-3.22.
   - At 1.5, 2 and 4 °C it is 4.11, 5.57 and 9.39 times as often.
   - The two research briefs gave different ranges. Both are in the CSV, so always name which range is shown.
   - The 3.0 °C row (8.12) is not in the published figure; say so if it is shown.
   - Never call the 1 °C column "today". Human-induced warming reached 1.37 °C in 2025 (IGCC), and observed warming for 2016-2025 was 1.26 °C.
   - The drought panel covers "drying regions" and is based on AR6 Figure 11.18. The briefs disagree on whether that is 16 or 17 regions; count them from the README before publishing.
2. **"Observed and attributed" card** (open, SPM.3 data on CEDA, version v20221116). I recounted the CSVs:

   | Extreme | Increased | Decreased | Low agreement | Limited data | Human contribution: high / medium confidence |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|
   | Hot extremes | 41 of 45 regions | – | 2 | 2 | 23 / 16 |
   | Heavy rain | 19 | – | 8 | 18 | 1 / 1 |
   | Agricultural and ecological drought | 12 | 1 | 28 | 4 | 0 / 2 |

   - Show world-level counts only, with the "calculated from the IPCC data" credit for anything the IPCC did not print.
3. **Heat where people live:**
   - Lancet 1.1.1 (noncommercial, CC BY-NC-SA): in 2024 about 31 heatwave days per person, about 26 of them attributable to climate change. Show 2020-2024 as a short end segment, not a trend.
   - Quilcaille et al. 2025 (CC BY), as text only: +1.4, +1.7 and +2.2 °C for the heatwaves of 2000-09, 2010-19 and 2020-23.
4. **Rain and drought, with the IPCC caveat printed beside them:**
   - Lancet 1.2.3, extreme rainfall: about 3.7 days a year in 1961-1990 against 4.3 in 2015-2024. Show the 1991-1994 gap as a gap.
   - Lancet 1.2.2, drought.
5. **Toll on people, all labelled as recorded counts:**
   - CRED Disasters in Numbers 2025 (CC BY), one edition only: 358 disasters, 16,607 deaths, against a 2005-2024 average of 377 disasters and 57,429 deaths. The 2025 extreme-temperature deaths are not yet counted.
   - IDMC displacement 2008-2025 (CC BY-NC-SA). These are movements, not people.
   - Formetta & Feyen 2019 (CC BY) as the context line: death rates among exposed people fell about 6.5-fold.
   - Newman & Noy 2023 (CC BY): about US$143 billion a year attributable, range 58-228 billion, labelled modelled.
   - United States page only: NOAA billion-dollar disasters (1980-2024), NWS fatalities, NOAA Climate Extremes Index.

## 2. What must never be claimed

- **Recorded disaster counts do not show that disasters are becoming more frequent, or that climate change is the cause.** This covers EM-DAT/CRED, IDMC, the Global Flood Database event list, and counts of Carbon Brief or World Weather Attribution studies. They track reporting, monitoring effort and research effort. CRED's own 2025 numbers are below the 20-year average.
- **Rising losses do not prove a climate signal.** NOAA's US$1 billion count and costs are not adjusted for growth in people and property in harm's way.
- **Trend series do not prove attribution.** Marine heatwave days, TXx, CCKP, Lancet 1.2.2 and 1.2.3, and the NOAA index are "observed trend" only. "Due to climate change" may only come from SPM.3, SPM.6, the A.3.x quotes, Lancet 1.1.1, Quilcaille, or the Met Office studies.
- **Hurricanes and storms are not "more frequent".** AR6 has low confidence in long-term trends in tropical cyclone frequency. It finds only that the proportion of category 3-5 storms likely increased (A.3.4, quote only).
- **No global flood trend.** AR6 has low confidence in global flood trends.
- **No "global drought driven by climate change".** The IPCC's confidence in a human contribution is medium, and only in some regions.
- **No "global wildfire area rising".** Global burned area has fallen, mainly in savannas, even as fire weather worsened. State of Wildfires gives regional results only.
- **No "disasters kill more people than ever".**
- **Modelled values are not observed.** Do not turn warming levels into years or a time series, interpolate a 1.37 °C value, or apply SPM.6 or SPM.3 regions to countries.
- **No splicing or mixing.** Do not add Climate Central onto NOAA, join CRED editions, splice in the Lancet 2026 vintage, join the marine heatwave mean column across 1982, or combine single-event attribution studies into a series.
- **No charts or data files from no-derivatives or display-only sources.** This covers Carbon Brief, World Weather Attribution, the WMO Atlas, and the IPCC SPM text and artwork.

## 3. Open sources nobody had checked (licences checked here)

- **NOAA IBTrACS v04r01** (doi:10.25921/82ty-9e16), global tropical cyclone tracks from 1842. The NCEI ISO metadata gives only "Use Constraints: Cite as: Gahtan, Jennifer; Knapp, Kenneth R.; … (2024)" and a "Distribution liability: NOAA and NCEI make no warranty…" disclaimer, with no restriction. That makes it a US federal open source.
  - Its value is as a guardrail: it shows no clean rise in the *number* of storms.
  - Do not chart counts before the satellite era, which are undercounts. Do not compute a share of major storms, because intensities differ between agencies.
  - Best uses: event callouts on country pages, plus the A.3.4 quote.
- **Grant et al. 2025, Nature 641, doi:10.1038/s41586-025-08907-1.** Crossref and the article both say CC BY 4.0: "Open Access This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License".
  - **This is a projection, so label it projected/modelled (ISIMIP2b).** Under a 1.5 °C pathway, 52% of people born in 2020 will experience unprecedented lifetime exposure to heatwaves; at 3.5 °C by 2100 it is 92%.
  - It suits a "children born today" drill-down.
- **Global Flood Database (Tellman et al. 2021).** The Earth Engine catalogue says: "This work is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution Non Commercial 4.0 International license." It holds 913 events from 2000-2018, static.
  - The events were chosen from Dartmouth Flood Observatory reports, so counts are not a frequency trend.
  - Low priority. If used at all, it would only support a context statement about more people living in flood-exposed areas.
